introduction.text: In this lesson, you will learn common Spanish proverbs and sayings that reflect cultural wisdom and values. These expressions often convey deeper meanings and can enhance your conversational skills.
introduction.culturalNote: Proverbs are an essential part of Spanish-speaking cultures, often passed down through generations. They can reveal cultural attitudes and social norms.

vocabulary.definition: It’s preferable to do something late than not do it at all.

exampleSentence.original: Decidí ir a la fiesta, más vale tarde que nunca.
exampleSentence.translation: I decided to go to the party, better late than never.

vocabulary.tip: Use this phrase to encourage someone who is hesitating to take action.

vocabulary.term: el que no llora, no mama
vocabulary.translation: he who doesn't cry, doesn't suck
vocabulary.definition: You must ask for what you want; otherwise, you won’t receive it.
vocabulary.pronunciation: el keh noh yoh-rah, noh mah-mah

exampleSentence.original: Si no pides un aumento, el que no llora, no mama.
exampleSentence.translation: If you don't ask for a raise, he who doesn't cry, doesn't suck.

vocabulary.tip: This expression emphasizes the importance of being assertive.

vocabulary.term: no hay mal que por bien no venga
vocabulary.translation: every cloud has a silver lining
vocabulary.definition: Every negative situation can lead to positive outcomes.
vocabulary.pronunciation: noh eye mahl keh por byen noh ven-gah

exampleSentence.original: Aunque perdí mi trabajo, no hay mal que por bien no venga.
exampleSentence.translation: Although I lost my job, every cloud has a silver lining.

vocabulary.tip: Use this proverb to comfort someone going through tough times.

vocabulary.term: a buen hambre no hay mal pan
vocabulary.translation: to a good hunger, there is no bad bread
vocabulary.definition: When you are really in need, you will accept whatever is available.
vocabulary.pronunciation: ah buen ahm-breh noh eye mahl pahn

exampleSentence.original: En situaciones difíciles, a buen hambre no hay mal pan.
exampleSentence.translation: In difficult situations, to a good hunger, there is no bad bread.

vocabulary.tip: This saying can be used to highlight pragmatism in desperate situations.

vocabulary.definition: Too much familiarity can lead to disrespect.

exampleSentence.original: Recuerda que donde hay confianza, da asco.

vocabulary.tip: Use this proverb to caution against becoming too comfortable with someone.

vocabulary.term: el que mucho abarca, poco aprieta
vocabulary.translation: he who grasps too much holds little
vocabulary.definition: If you try to do too much, you may not succeed at anything.
vocabulary.pronunciation: el keh moo-choh ah-bar-kah, poh-koh ah-preh-tah

exampleSentence.original: Si quieres hacer varios proyectos, recuerda que el que mucho abarca, poco aprieta.
exampleSentence.translation: If you want to undertake several projects, remember that he who grasps too much holds little.

vocabulary.tip: This saying advises moderation and focus.

grammar.title: Subjunctive in Proverb Usage
grammar.explanation: Many Spanish proverbs imply conditional or hypothetical situations, often requiring the subjunctive mood. The subjunctive expresses wishes, doubts, or non-real actions. In proverbs, this is usually implicit but essential for understanding nuances.

examples.original: Si el que no llora, no mama, es que no pide.
examples.translation: If he who doesn't cry doesn't suck, it means he doesn't ask.
examples.breakdown: This uses the subjunctive to express a general truth.

commonMistakes: Using the indicative instead of the subjunctive in hypothetical expressions.
Failing to recognize when to use 'que' before the subjunctive.

dialogue.title: Discussing Challenges and Proverbs
dialogue.context: A conversation between two friends at a café discussing their recent challenges.

lines.text: Últimamente he estado preocupado por mi trabajo.
lines.translation: Lately, I've been worried about my job.
lines.note: Laura opens up about her concerns.

lines.text: No te preocupes, recuerda que más vale tarde que nunca.
lines.translation: Don't worry, remember that better late than never.

lines.text: Sí, pero siento que el tiempo se me acaba.
lines.translation: Yes, but I feel like time is running out.

lines.text: A veces pienso que no hay mal que por bien no venga.
lines.translation: Sometimes I think that every cloud has a silver lining.

lines.text: Eso es cierto, pero es difícil ver el lado positivo.
lines.translation: That’s true, but it’s hard to see the positive side.

lines.text: Exacto, el que mucho abarca, poco aprieta, así que enfócate en lo esencial.
lines.translation: Exactly, he who grasps too much holds little, so focus on the essentials.

lines.text: Tienes razón, debo priorizar mis tareas.
lines.translation: You're right, I need to prioritize my tasks.

lines.text: Y recuerda que el que no llora, no mama.
lines.translation: And remember that he who doesn’t cry, doesn’t suck.

culture.title: The Role of Proverbs in Spanish Culture
culture.text: Proverbs are often used in everyday conversations in Spanish-speaking cultures to convey wisdom and life lessons. They are a way to express complex ideas succinctly and are frequently employed in literature and oral storytelling.
culture.funFact: In many cultures, including Spanish-speaking ones, proverbs evolve over time, leading to variations that reflect local customs and experiences.

keyPoints: Understanding the meaning and usage of common Spanish proverbs.
Recognizing the importance of the subjunctive mood in expressing hypothetical situations.
Applying proverbs in everyday conversations to enhance communication.
Cultural significance of proverbs in expressing values and wisdom.
summary.nextSteps: Practice using these proverbs in your conversations. Try to incorporate them into your writing or speaking exercises to reinforce your learning.

exercises.question: What does 'más vale tarde que nunca' mean?

options: The early bird catches the worm
All good things come to those who wait

exercises.explanation: 'Más vale tarde que nunca' translates to 'Better late than never', implying that it's better to do something late than not at all.
exercises.hint: Think about the value of timing.

exercises.question: Which proverb means 'The one who does not cry, does not suck'?

options: El que no llora, no mama
No hay mal que por bien no venga
A buen hambre no hay mal pan

exercises.explanation: This proverb emphasizes that one must ask for what they want to receive it.
exercises.hint: Focus on the idea of asking for help.

exercises.question: Complete the proverb: 'No hay mal que por ___ no venga.'

content.sentence: No hay mal que por ___ no venga.

exercises.explanation: The correct answer is 'bien', which completes the saying that suggests that bad situations may lead to good outcomes.
exercises.hint: Think about how bad events can have positive results.

exercises.question: Finish this saying: 'A buen hambre no hay ___ pan.'

content.sentence: A buen hambre no hay ___ pan.

exercises.explanation: The phrase translates to 'When you are hungry, there is no such thing as bad bread', meaning that in desperate situations, people are less picky.
exercises.hint: Consider the context of hunger and needs.

exercises.question: Rearrange the words to form a correct saying: 'poco abarca, el que mucho'

content.translation: He who tries to do too much ends up doing little.

exercises.explanation: This proverb warns against overextending oneself.

exercises.question: Translate to Spanish: 'Where there is trust, it is disgusting.'

content.prompt: Translate to Spanish: 'Where there is trust, it is disgusting.'

exercises.explanation: This saying implies that familiarity can lead to a lack of respect.
exercises.hint: Focus on trust and its consequences.

exercises.question: Listen and choose the correct translation: 'Donde hay confianza, da asco.'

options: Where there is trust, it is disgusting.
Where there is trust, there is love.

exercises.explanation: The correct translation captures the essence of the Spanish proverb.
exercises.hint: Think about the negative side of trust.

acceptableVariants: El que no llora no mama
El que no llora, no mamas

exercises.explanation: This saying emphasizes the need to ask for what you want to receive it.
